Meeting header:

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
Redwood team walked through multi-hop latency profile, differences between streaming and non-streaming for their chat endpoints, KV cache hotspotting, and batching/quantization tradeoffs. Action items were assigned to share traces, run on-prem benchmarks, and review security docs.

Topics: p95/p99 tail attribution; streaming vs non-streaming; network hop delta; KV cache hotkeys and sharding; batching window tuning; quantization impact on latency and tail; VPC/on-prem networking considerations; KMS/HSM and key fetch latency.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hi everyone, thanks for making time, um, we wanted to focus today on the p95/p99 behaviour you've been seeing and dig into root causes, so Priya and Tomás will take the technical lead.
[00:18] Marcus: Yeah, great, uh, thanks. We've been seeing, like, pretty good median numbers for generation but the tail is killing us — our internal SLA is 250ms p95 and 500ms p99, and in production the p99 is spiking to ~800–1,200ms for some routes.
[00:35] Priya: okay, and is that across streaming endpoints or non-streaming? just want to scope.
[00:42] Leila: Mostly their newer chat api is streaming enabled but we also have non-streaming fallbacks for batch jobs. The worst spikes are on streaming session handoffs when the convo context is large.
[00:55] Tomás: right, common pattern — once the KV cache lookup path touches a hot key and the request goes multi-hop (app -> vpc peering -> redwood private node -> kv shard -> gpu node), you pick up 3 to 4 network hops. Each hop adds variable latency, often 5–25ms depending on routing and peering, and that variability blows out the p99.
[01:18] Omar: yeah we're seeing a lot of KV cache misses when two parallel clients hit the same conversation id — hotkey syndrome.
[01:24] Priya: a few immediate things to consider: prefix/KV caching for the most common prefixes so you avoid the first miss penalty, and sharding hot keys across multiple KV backends. also auto-warming the prefix cache on deploys.
[01:38] Marcus: quick question — how much does streaming actually help the tail versus non-streaming? we've assumed streaming reduces p99 because it starts token emission earlier.
[01:47] Priya: it's nuanced — streaming can reduce time-to-first-byte substantially, which helps perceived latency. but for p99 of full generation it depends on where the stall occurs. If the stall is network (multi-hop), streaming helps little because you still need the first token's KV and kernel scheduling. if stall is model compute, streaming helps by overlapping compute and network, reducing the tail.
[02:12] Leila: so for our case where the spike is at the start of the request path (kv miss + peering), streaming maybe won't fix the p99.
[02:20] Tomás: exactly, and we measured anecdotally — for similar configs, median improved 15–25% with streaming but p99 only improved 5–10% when network hops dominate. We'll share the trace.
[02:34] Alex: I'll drop the trace link in the follow up: https://redwood.link/vg-latency-deck and there's a live profiling gist.
[02:44] Nadia: on security, we need to confirm that adding prefix caching doesn't surface any PII or residual context — our compliance team is adamant about redaction before caching.
[02:54] Priya: yep, recommended to use deterministic hashing + metadata-only caching for sensitive prefixes; Redwood Private supports per-tenant prefix policies and an allowlist for non-cacheable keys.
[03:06] Marcus: can you walk through the breakdown you typically show — where to measure token-level latency?
[03:12] Tomás: sure — we break latency into: client RTT, ingress routing, KV lookup, model startup (kernel load + warmup), decoding/kv-merge, token generation, and egress/stream chunking. In our tooling we often see KV lookup and kernel scheduling as the biggest contributors to tail.
[03:36] Marcus: numbers? like, ballpark for our setup?
[03:40] Tomás: ballpark: client RTT 10–30ms, ingress 5–15ms, KV lookup 20–200ms depending on hotkey and whether it's local or cross-az, model startup 30–80ms (cold kernels), token generation per-token ~5–15ms depending on model size and quantization. But the kicker is variability on KV and kernel scheduling — they inflate p99.
[04:03] Omar: we run larger context windows — often 8k tokens or more — does that significantly change tail?
[04:08] Priya: larger context increases KV pressure and KV lookup cost, plus memory pressure on the GPU can cause extra kernel pages and stalls. For long context we recommend aggressive prefix caching and also quantization profiles tailored for longer sequences.
[04:24] Marcus: about quantization — we tried int8 and saw lower avg latency but some jitter and rare decode artifacts. Thoughts?
[04:33] Tomás: int8 usually reduces compute time 20–40% but can change kernel layout leading to variance in tail. With our runtime we choose kernels that minimize jitter; however you might still see a few outliers if the int8 path triggers different memory access patterns. We recommend a canary run with your prompt set and to monitor quality metrics.
[04:55] Leila: what about batching — we do a mix of single-turn chat and batch summarization jobs. Batching helps cost but hurts single-request latency, correct?
[05:02] Priya: yes — batching increases throughput and amortizes kernel startup, but for SLOged interactive paths you want small/elastic batching windows or maintain a hot pool of ready GPU workers (or reserved capacity) to avoid queuing delay. Redwood Dedicated (they called it "Redwood Dedicate" at one point in notes) supports reserved pools and configurable max wait windows.
[05:24] Marcus: can autoscaling contribute to p99 spikes? we do scale-to-zero for cost reasons sometimes.
[05:29] Tomás: yes — scale events produce cold kernels and cache coldness; we typically recommend a small always-on footprint for critical interactive endpoints, or pre-warm on scheduled traffic spikes. Also lazy-compilation can add 30–200ms on first traffic.
[05:43] Omar: network hops — how do we quantify the effect of our VPC peering versus direct private link?
[05:49] Priya: we ran side-by-side tests — VPC peering often adds a few ms but depending on transit can add jitter; direct private link (express-route like) reduces variable routing and cuts 5–15ms tail and stabilizes p99. For on-prem, a direct private connect is strongly recommended.
[06:05] Nadia: and KMS/HSM? our security team wants HSM for key ops — any latency implications?
[06:10] Tomás: KMS/HSM calls usually happen during tokenization/key exchange not on each token; with caching of decrypted session keys the steady-state impact is minimal. If you configure envelope encryption with per-request key fetches you'd see 5–15ms overhead per request, but that's avoidable with session caching.
[06:25] Marcus: ok, what immediate experiments should we run? I'm keen to see a regression-proof plan.
[06:30] Priya: suggest these experiments in parallel: 1) reproduce p99 locally with profiling script (we'll supply) 2) run a VPC peering vs private link latency test 3) enable prefix-only cache for sensitive prefixes 4) canary int8 quantization on non-critical routes 5) reserve a small Dedicated pool for chat SLOs.
[06:52] Leila: for the prefix cache we need a checklist for PII redaction — can you provide that?
[06:58] Alex: yes, we'll include a redaction checklist in the security packet.
[07:03] Marcus: do you have any quick wins we can do in the next 48 hours?
[07:07] Tomás: yes — tune batching window to 10–20ms for interactive routes, reduce pre-fetch timeouts and pin a tiny 2-node KV replica to the same AZ to reduce cross-az hops; both are low-risk config changes.
[07:20] Omar: is there an open-source profiler you recommend?
[07:23] Priya: we'll share a small python harness and trace collector — it emits per-segment timings and a p99 flamegraph. that's the profiling script I mentioned earlier.
[07:32] Nadia: do we need any paperwork for on-prem access or peering?
[07:36] Alex: we'll send the standard network onboarding doc and a SOC2 summary; we'll also note support for HSM integration + sample config.
[07:45] Marcus: okay let's recap next steps.
[07:48] Priya: recap: we will share profiler and p99 flamegraph; Vanguard to run baseline with existing peering; Redwood to spin up a small canary Dedicated pool and provide quantization numbers; security docs to be shared.
[07:58] Leila: and timeline? we'd like results before end of next week.
[08:02] Alex: sounds doable — aim for 2026-03-27 internal results and follow-up call week of 2026-03-30.
[08:10] Marcus: awesome thanks, that was very useful.
[08:13] Tomás: quick note, I'll attach a short doc on KV sharding patterns and a sample config for the KV client to reduce hotkey contention.
[08:21] Omar: perfect, thanks everyone.
